newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgaria to vote amid deep economic crisis.
newsitem.headline: Bulgaria to vote amid deep economic crisis.

text.p: Bulgarians vote on Sunday in the Balkan country's second presidential election since the end of communist rule, but most voters are more concerned with the deep economic crisis. Following are key facts about Bulgaria:
POPULATION: 8.38 million (1995), of which 7.2 million are Bulgarians, 800,000 ethnic Turks, 300,000 Gypsies and 100,000 others.
AREA: 110,994 sq km (42,855 sq miles). Bulgaria is bordered by Romania to the north, the Black Sea to the east, Greece and Turkey to the south, and former Yugoslavia to the west.
LANGUAGE: The official language is Bulgarian.
RELIGION: Eastern Orthodoxy is practised by 86.6 percent of Bulgarians. Some 13.1 percent of the population are Moslems, and the remainder practise other faiths.

ARMED FORCES: Active forces: 51,600 (about 33,300 conscripts), including some 22,300 centrally controlled, 3,400 Defence Ministry staff, but excluding some 10,000 construction troops. Term of service: 18 months. Reserves: 303,000. Army: 51,600 (33,300 conscripts). Navy 3,000 (2,000 conscripts). Air Force 21,600 (16,000 conscripts). (Source: International Insitute of Strategic Studies).

ECONOMY: Bulgaria has been slow to implement politically unpopular reforms and has the lowest level of foreign investment in the region. The lev has collapsed from 70 to the dollar at the beginning of the year to about 230 now and the government has filed insolvency suits against five local banks and placed another nine in receivership.

In 1995, Bulgaria's GDP totalled 871.4 billion levs, a rise of 2.6 percent in real terms over 1994. GDP is expected to be negative this year. In September 1996 10.4 percent of the workforce were unemployed. Inflation is expected to exceed 200 percent by year end. Foreign exchange reserves fell to $506 million at end-September from $575 million in August, and $1.47 billion in September 1995.

HISTORY: For 500 years until the late 19th century, Bulgaria was part of the Ottoman Empire. After the war between Russia and Turkey in 1878, the northern part of the country gained its independence, while the south remained an autonomous Turkish province. The two were united peacefully in 1885. The country became a constitutional monarchy in 1879 with the adoption of its first constitution. By 1945 Bulgaria had taken part in three wars (the Balkan wars of 1912-13, World War One and World War Two) and had lost all of them. In 1944, with the help of the Soviet army, the Bulgarian Communist Party took power and ruled as the single party until 1989. The monarchy was abolished through a referendum in 1946, though exiled King Simeon drew huge crowds when he arrived for a month-long visit in May 1996.

On November 10, 1989 communist dictator Todor Zhivkov was ousted by other top party officials led by Foreign Minister Petar Mladenov, who later became president. The former Communists reformed as the Socialist Party and won a sweeping victory in the first democratic parliamentary election in June 1990. Mladenov resigned as president in July 1990 amid widespread anti-government protests and parliament elected opposition leader Zhelyu Zhelev president the following month. Zhelev, a prominent dissident, was one of the founders of the Union of Democratic Forces, an anti-communist coalition. Zhelev won the first presidential election in January, 1992.

In 1990, Mladenov appointed Andrei Lukanov prime minister but he was forced out of office by strikes and student protests and in December 1990 the socialist-dominated parliament formed a coalition government headed by non-party lawyer Dimitar Popov and including UDF members. The government endorsed a programme of tough economic reforms and prepared an early election in autumn 1991. The UDF won a modest majority in parliament and formed a government which was ousted in a no-confidence vote after only 11 months in power. It was replaced by a non-party government backed by the Bulgarian Socialist Party and the Movement for Rights and Freedoms, representing most ethnic Turks. This government, led by Luyben Berov, resigned in September 1994 amid accusations that it was delaying reforms. Elections in December 1994 gave the Socialists a parliamentary majority but critics of Zhan Videnov's government say it has been no more successful at resolving the crisis and accuse it of dragging its feet on economic reforms prescribed by the International Monetary Fund.
